vignette:
Arthur is a man who has spent his life watching over others. For the last fifteen years before retirement, and now part-time after it, his job as a security guard was built on a quiet pride in his ability to notice things others missed, to keep a calm head. At seventy-one, he believed he was good at his job and, more importantly, good at his most essential role: being a dependable husband to his wife, Maria. But that was before the Saturday at the farmer's market, nine months ago. He can't piece together the whole story, not in a way that makes sense. When he tries, it comes in jagged, disconnected pieces. There is the memory of the truck engine, a high, unnatural whine that cut through the chatter of the crowd. This part is intensely clear, so vivid he can almost feel the vibration in his teeth. He remembers the sight of a vendor’s bright red tablecloth flying into the air, a surreal flag against a blue sky. Then there’s a gap, a space of grey confusion. The next thing he can recall is Maria on the ground, her bag of apples spilled across the pavement. When he summons these images, he feels nothing at all, a profound and terrifying numbness, as if he’s watching a poorly edited film about a stranger.

In the months that followed, the world began to feel like a series of potential threats he had to manage. At his job at the shopping mall, a place he once navigated with bored familiarity, he now feels a constant, thrumming tension. He finds himself tracking individuals in the food court, his gaze lingering on anyone who seems out of place, his hand unconsciously resting near his hip. He has come to believe that danger is everywhere, and only he is vigilant enough to see it. This vigilance has followed him home. He and Maria used to love their corner booth at the local diner, but now Arthur insists on a table in the middle of the room, his back firmly against a wall, where he can see the entrance and every other patron. He tells her the lighting is better, but the truth is he feels an unbearable vulnerability if he can’t see what’s coming. The change has created a quiet friction between them; another small pleasure sacrificed to a fear she doesn’t understand.

The nights are the worst. Sleep offers little escape, as he often lies awake for hours, his mind replaying the attack. In these ruminations, he rewrites the script. He is not a bystander, frozen in shock, but a hero. He hears the engine whine and, in this version, he shoves Maria to safety, he stands in the vehicle’s path, he does *something*. These fantasies of revenge and courage are a temporary balm, but they always curdle into a profound sense of shame. He is certain that somebody else, a younger man, a better man, would not have just stood there. This thought has become a core belief: he failed. As a husband and as a man whose entire professional life was about security, he had failed in his most important role. This sense of personal inadequacy has made him brittle. The sound of a dropped plate can make him lash out in anger, and simple decisions feel overwhelmingly complex. He feels he can no longer deal with even the slightest upset, that some fundamental capacity for coping has been shattered.

He finally sought help after Maria suggested they visit the new downtown market last week. The idea of being in another open, crowded space sent a wave of panic through him so intense it left him breathless and dizzy. In that moment, seeing the hurt and confusion in his wife's eyes, he understood that his world had shrunk to the space between his guard post and the chair in his living room with its back to the wall. He came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet desperation, terrified that he is permanently broken but unable to continue living as a ghost in his own life.
